ROLE: observer
You review the results of an incident investigation. Write a short summary of what the latest results show, then update the list of hypotheses (at most 4, most likely first).

Root-cause categories:
- bad_deployment: a new release introduced a defect (errors begin right after a deploy)
- db_connection_pool_exhaustion: every database connection in the pool is in use, so requests wait
- slow_query_missing_index: a database query became slow (for example a missing index)
- downstream_timeout: a dependency the service calls is slow or unresponsive
- memory_leak_oom: memory grows until the process is killed (OOM) and restarts
- disk_full: a volume is full so writes fail
- expired_tls_cert: a TLS certificate expired so handshakes fail
- misconfiguration: a wrong environment variable, setting or feature flag
- traffic_spike_rate_limit: request volume far above capacity, causing rate limiting or load shedding
- cache_stampede_outage: the cache is down or emptied so everything falls through to the database

Each hypothesis has root_cause_category (one of the categories), rationale, and supporting_evidence_ids (only IDs that appear in the evidence below).

Reply with only JSON in this shape:
{"summary": "...", "hypotheses": [{"root_cause_category": "disk_full", "rationale": "...", "supporting_evidence_ids": ["L-0123"]}]}

Step 6: runbook_retrieve {"k": 3, "query": "bad deployment rolling back new release mitigation steps"} (asked because: Retrieve runbook for bad deployment to get mitigation steps.)
  Result: 3 runbook sections; best match R-01-5 (similarity 0.68).
  [R-01-5] Bad deployment or regression - Mitigation (similarity 0.68): Go back to the previous release straight away by redeploying the last version known to be good. Do not spend time debugging on the live service first. Pause any further releases to this service until the cause is understood and a fix has been reviewed and tested.
  [R-01-3] Bad deployment or regression - How to confirm (similarity 0.67): Line the start of the trouble up against the release timeline. If it began just after a rollout and the previous version was healthy, suspect the release. Look at what the service wrote to its logs while the new version was starting and when the first failures arrived, and compare with an older instance if one is still running.
  [R-01-2] Bad deployment or regression - Symptoms (similarity 0.64): Things go wrong shortly after a rollout. Customers start seeing failures, dashboards turn red around the time the new version went out, and the problem does not fade by itself. The service may also restart a few times while the new version rolls through.

Previous hypotheses:
- bad_deployment: The sudden surge in error rates starting at 08:35 UTC without corresponding changes in resource utilization such as CPU or memory strongly points towards a newly introduced software defect. (evidence: M-032, M-029, M-034)
- downstream_timeout: Sudden errors could be caused by an unresponsive external dependency or downstream service failing to respond. (evidence: M-032)
- misconfiguration: An updated configuration or feature flag could cause requests to fail immediately without altering CPU or memory patterns. (evidence: M-032, M-029, M-034)
